dnsbl.score_collateral: Only {count} collateral listing(s) (subnet or dynamic range), not counted
dnsbl.score_domain: Domain listed on a domain blocklist (Spamhaus DBL, SURBL)
dnsbl.skip_no_ipv4: No public IPv4 address to check (DNS blocklists are queried by IPv4)
dnsbl.unreachable: DNS blocklists unreachable (timeouts or failing resolver)
finding.dnsbl.domain_listed: The domain {domain} is on domain blocklists ({zones}): {categories}.
finding.dnsbl.ip_listed: The IP address {ip} is on {count} DNS blocklist(s): {zones}.
finding.dnsbl.mail_listed: The mail server {host} ({ip}) is on {count} DNS blocklist(s): {zones}. Emails may be rejected.
module.dnsbl.checks: Queries about twenty DNS blocklists (Spamhaus, SpamCop, Barracuda, UCEPROTECT, DroneBL…) for the site's address and its mail servers' addresses, plus the Spamhaus DBL and SURBL domain lists. Refusal answers from public resolvers and dead zones are discarded.
module.dnsbl.fix:
Identify what is listed: the website's address, the address of a mail server (MX) or the domain itself, along with the blocklists named in the finding.
Check each listing with the commands in the snippet, from a DNS resolver of your own (blocklists refuse open public resolvers): write the address backwards in front of the blocklist name (`203.0.113.10` becomes `10.113.0.203`); a domain is written as is. `127.0.0.x` means "listed", `NXDOMAIN` means "not listed", `127.255.255.x` means "query refused", which is not a listing.
If a server is listed, look for the cause first: hijacked mailbox, compromised server, open relay, website form or script abused to send mail, malware. Examine the outgoing queue and the send logs, change the mail account passwords, close the relay, update the system and clean it before any removal request.
Put the mail setup in order: ask the host or the owner of the address range for reverse DNS (a PTR record) that points to a name in your domain, make the server's HELO/EHLO name identical to it and resolving to the same address, and publish SPF, DKIM and DMARC for the domain.
If the address is shared or was taken over from a former customer (shared hosting, VPS, dynamic range), or if the listing is only "collateral" (a whole subnet or range), the fault may not be yours: ask the host to deal with the abuse or to give you another address.
If the domain is on Spamhaus DBL or SURBL, the domain itself is flagged (phishing, malware, spam, hacked site): remove the malicious pages and files, secure the site (updates, passwords, unknown accounts), then move on to the next step.
Once the cause is fixed, request removal on the website of each blocklist concerned, explaining what you fixed; many lists also drop an address on their own after a few days without new abuse. For Spamhaus, the reputation checker at `check.spamhaus.org` details the listing (observed HELO values, reverse DNS checks) and guides the removal request.
Check again with the commands in the snippet, let the DNS cache expire, then run the DomainRecon scan again.
module.dnsbl.fix_snippet:
# dig
dig +short 10.113.0.203.zen.spamhaus.org A
dig +short 10.113.0.203.bl.spamcop.net A
dig +short 10.113.0.203.b.barracudacentral.org A
dig +short example.com.dbl.spamhaus.org A
dig +short -x 203.0.113.10
# PowerShell
Resolve-DnsName -Name 10.113.0.203.zen.spamhaus.org -Type A -DnsOnly
Resolve-DnsName -Name 10.113.0.203.bl.spamcop.net -Type A -DnsOnly
Resolve-DnsName -Name 10.113.0.203.in-addr.arpa -Type PTR -DnsOnly
module.dnsbl.title: DNS blocklists (DNSBL)
module.dnsbl.why: A listed address or domain sees its emails rejected or filed as spam and its traffic blocked by many firewalls: this is often the sign of a compromised server or an abusive hosting neighbour.
